bad: Care widens the room people have to think and act.
good: Care means people can decide, disagree and act without you in the room.
why: Dead spatial metaphor ('widens the room'); deleting it leaves a gap, so expand into concrete actor behavior while keeping 'room' literal.

bad: The restructuring that was right on paper still landed as a threat.
good: Silence at the all-hands was not agreement.
why: Stock-pair headline mixing two clichés ('on paper' + 'landed as'); state the concrete scene event instead.

bad: The levels move together.
good: A change of task is also a change of feeling and of reward.
why: Empty declarative transition that carries zero concrete detail; name what actually changes together.

bad: Gianpiero Petriglieri asks what a company does to people whose sense of who they are is still being formed. His answer: leadership happens where meaning, belonging and direction get made. Manfred Kets de Vries asks what happens when leaders and followers slide into old patterns: the leader gets adored, leaned on and feared. Both sides usually cannot see the pattern they are in.
good: Gianpiero Petriglieri starts from the person. He asks what a company does to people whose sense of who they are is still being formed, and his answer is that leadership happens where meaning, belonging and direction get made. Manfred Kets de Vries looks at the bond between leader and follower: when the two fall into old patterns, the leader adored, leaned on and feared, neither side usually sees the pattern they are in.
why: Mirrored 'First Last asks...' frames in the same paragraph sound templated; vary opening shape and sentence rhythm.

bad: Holding is not soothing.
good: Holding means staying with a hard reality without pretending it will pass.
why: Leading negation forces the reader to guess the positive claim; state what it is directly.

bad: Nobody is told how people will be selected.
good: HR never states who will be let go, or by what criteria.
why: Passive voice hides the actor who stayed silent; put the responsible actor in the subject.

bad: Good tools remind us that simplicity always wins in the end.
good: The bash script is 73 lines long and runs in two seconds.
why: Poster-ready closing moral ('simplicity always wins') with no regex-banned word; end on a concrete measurable fact instead.

bad: Put two researchers in that room and the silence changes meaning.
good: If you put two researchers in that room, the silence changes meaning.
why: Imperative opener reads like a command rather than an observation; frame advice as a conditional.

bad: În vederea finalizării proiectului, echipa va efectua o analiză și va furniza datele ulterior.
good: Ca să terminăm proiectul, echipa verifică cifrele și trimite raportul vineri.
why: Romanian bureaucratic Latinisms ('în vederea', 'efectua', 'furniza', 'ulterior'); write the sentence as spoken to a colleague.

bad: Il convient d'effectuer une vérification approfondie en vue de pérenniser le dispositif.
good: Il faut vérifier le système cette semaine pour qu'il tienne dans la durée.
why: Formal French administrative register ('il convient de', 'effectuer', 'en vue de', 'pérenniser'); replace with plain spoken verbs.

bad: Good leadership means balancing empathy with accountability across every level of the organization.
good: A manager has to hear what worries the team and still cut the project that loses money.
why: Press-release abstraction ('balancing empathy with accountability') uses zero banned regex words yet says nothing concrete; name the exact conflicting actions.

bad: He starts from the person, asking what a company does to people whose sense of who they are is still forming. His answer is that leadership happens where people make meaning, belonging, and direction.
good: When the chief executive refuses to name the criteria for cuts, people in the room hear a threat to their livelihood, their craft, and their place at work. Gianpiero Petriglieri studies how employees protect themselves and go quiet when an organisation threatens who they are.
why: Avoid chained A->B->C rhetorical progressions ('starts from... asking... his answer is...') and elliptical jumps; state directly how the researcher's work explains what just happened in the scene.

bad: If you put two researchers in that room, the silence stops looking like a messaging problem. It starts looking like a question about what a decision does to the people in it.
good: Two INSEAD researchers explain why the room goes silent after a restructuring announcement and why the chief executive misreads that silence as agreement.
why: Disguised leading negation ('stops looking like X; it starts looking like Y') combined with a dead visual metaphor ('silence looks like') and no explicit causal link.

bad: Three people ask, in the chat and out loud. The word that comes back is resistance.
good: Three people ask, in the chat and out loud. The managers call those questions resistance, while the staff see the managers protecting themselves and keeping the rest of the room out.
why: Avoid elliptical 'The word that comes back is X' shorthand that hides who spoke and how both sides read the exchange; name the actors and their concrete reactions.

bad: The managers call those questions resistance, while the staff see the managers protecting themselves and keeping the rest of the room out. After that the chat goes quiet.
good: The managers in the front row call those questions resistance, and their tone shuts the thread down. To the staff behind them, the managers are protecting their own seats and keeping the rest of the room out. A cold silence settles over the twelfth floor. Nobody types. In the front rows, faces stiffen and jaws tighten; at the back, shoulders drop and hands grip phone edges and paper coffee cups. Resentment and insecurity sit in the warm air while the projector keeps humming.
why: Do not rush past a charged scene in one summary sentence; rest on the moment by describing the room, stiff faces, posture, sound, and mood.

bad: Two INSEAD researchers explain why the room goes silent after a restructuring announcement and why the chief executive misreads that silence as agreement.
good: Two INSEAD researchers explain what happens in the room after such an announcement and why a quiet room can hide a communication gap between management and staff.
why: Avoid repeating the same key noun ('silence') right after the previous paragraph and twice in the same sentence; vary with concrete phrasing.

bad: Together, their work gives a leader two needs that conflict with each other. Care means people can decide, disagree, and act without you in the room. Reality-testing keeps the leader in contact with what is happening.
good: In that twelfth-floor room, the two researchers look at the same problem from two different angles. Petriglieri focuses on care: people can decide, disagree, and act without the leader in the room. Kets de Vries focuses on reality-testing: keeping the leader in contact with what is actually happening.
why: Do not invent a 'conflict' between abstract ideas or facets; reserve 'conflict' for people and frame complementary lenses as two facets or angles.

bad: Reality-testing without care hands people hard facts with no way to bear the loss.
good: Reality-testing without care hands people hard facts with no way to sustain the loss.
why: Prefer 'sustain' or 'handle' over 'bear' unless referring to an actual bear.

bad: To the staff behind them, the managers are protecting their own seats. Resentment and insecurity sit in the warm air while the projector keeps humming.
good: A cold silence settles over the twelfth floor. Nobody types. In the front rows, faces stiffen and jaws tighten; at the back, shoulders drop and hands grip phone edges and paper coffee cups.
why: Do not mix levels in description mode: stay with observable behavior and physical room details, and leave motives or feeling names for the analysis.

bad: Soothing tries to quiet the room down; holding keeps people looking at the problem together.
good: It makes sense to distinguish between soothing and holding: soothing tries to quiet the room down, while holding keeps people looking at the problem together.
why: Do not start a paragraph with an unintroduced contrast or topic jump; open with a brief bridge explaining why the next distinction follows.

bad: Anthropic calls this three-stage loading pattern progressive disclosure, and its purpose is context hygiene rather than prompt cleverness.
good: Anthropic calls this three-stage loading pattern progressive disclosure, and its purpose is context hygiene.
why: Focus on what it is, not what it is not; cut filler 'rather than' contrast tails unless they express a cited author's substantive argument.

bad: Tiers 3 and 4 live in evals/: a 30-prompt routing CSV (triggers.csv) and A/B behavioral cases (cases.json + graders.py).
good: The higher verification tiers test routing with thirty prompts, including ten negative controls that must stay silent, and run A/B comparisons between unguided and skill-guided runs.
why: Filenames and script paths belong in tables or bullet lists; reserve narrative paragraphs for clear explanations and links to articles.

bad: Packaging taste as code, and knowing when the model will eat it
good: Packaging taste as code
why: A model cannot eat; replace the dead metaphor and over-explained phrasing with the literal question.

bad: Packaging taste as code, and what survives stronger models
good: Packaging taste as code
why: Keep titles short and direct; cut two-part ', and what...' AI suspense tails that over-explain the essay.

bad: The system did not start as a diagram; it grew out of arguments over concrete drafts.
good: The system grew out of arguments over concrete drafts across more than a week of sustained work.
why: Do not lead with or explain what something is not; state directly what it is and what happened.

bad: Yet that future collapses the moment the output reads like standard model prose.
good: Yet when the output reads like AI, it becomes quickly boring, stale, and attention dissipates.
why: Avoid abstract metaphors like 'future collapses'; state the concrete observable effect on the reader.

bad: I did not design those choices up front on a whiteboard; they emerged out of back-and-forth conversations with the AI.
good: Those choices emerged out of back-and-forth conversations with the AI, often in YOLO mode.
why: Never lead with or explain what you did not do; state directly what happened.

bad: The hardest tradeoff sits between deterministic code graders and model-based rubrics.
good: The main verification gap sits between deterministic code graders and model-based rubrics.
why: Cut 'hardest' on abstract tradeoffs when it does not convey personal hardship; name the concrete gap.

bad: Because personal writing and real-world verification sit outside closed games, three pieces stay useful.
good: Because personal writing and real-world fact checking lack the crisp win conditions of chess or Go, three pieces stay useful.
why: Never introduce an unexplained concept ('closed games'); state the concrete contrast directly.

bad: Every time I rejected a draft line during our editing sessions on November 19, 20, and 21, the agent logged the pair.
good: Every time I rejected a draft line over more than a week of building and editing, the agent logged the pair.
why: When the effort or duration is the point, state the duration rather than listing trivia calendar dates.

bad: design-system.md summarizes the palette (#FBFAF7 paper, #30332F ink, #8D2829 burgundy), typography, and tokens.css.
good: alexandru-style separates visual design from prose writing and validates rendered HTML against a passing sample and a failing anti-sample.
why: Focus architecture essays on roles and concepts; cut irrelevant hex colors, CSS token trivia, and exhaustive file lists.

bad: In today's fast-paced engineering landscape, teams must prioritize high-impact deliverables rather than glamorous initiatives, fostering a culture that rewards foundational work.
good: Sometimes we just need to work on the most impactful thing, even if it is boring. And we must encourage and reward that.
why: Replace corporate buzzwords (landscape, deliverables, fostering) with spoken words and state the tradeoff plainly.

bad: When a technical specification proves difficult to parse, the onus of facilitating seamless comprehension rests primarily with the document author rather than the reviewer.
good: If the design doc is hard to read, then there’s clearly a gap, because the responsibility for clear communication should be mostly at the emitter’s end and less at the receiver’s.
why: Cut Latinate nominalizations (facilitating seamless comprehension, onus); state who holds the responsibility in plain English.

bad: Unsustainable work schedules ultimately undermine software quality; consequently, engineering leadership must proactively mitigate overtime through upstream capacity planning.
good: Excessive overtime is an enemy of quality. Managers and teams should proactively estimate and find ways to diminish the need for long hours in the office and keep the project on track early.
why: Break one bureaucratic sentence into a short direct claim followed by what managers and teams actually do.

bad: Developing software in organizational silos inhibits psychological safety around course correction, preventing leadership from delving into root causes.
good: Developing in isolation makes it difficult for people to say 'STOP, we need to change this' and management never truly gets to the bottom of problems to fix them.
why: Replace abstract HR jargon (silos, inhibits psychological safety, delving) with what people actually say in the room.

bad: At the end of the day, production source code serves as the ultimate cornerstone of value creation within the software delivery lifecycle.
good: Code is closest to value in the value chain. Unless circumstances call for something else, and this should be the exception.
why: Cut filler openers and cornerstone metaphors; state the position and its exception directly.

bad: True craftsmanship does not exist in a vacuum; rather, it is underpinned by a profound, holistic commitment to understanding the end-user journey.
good: But a Craftsman is creating an object that is meant to be used by a person. To be a great craftsman, there must be a genuine interest for the end user.
why: Do not open with what craftsmanship is not or use weight/journey clichés; name the object and the person who uses it.

bad: In a globalized organization, evaluation frameworks must avoid inadvertently penalizing non-native speakers whose role profiles do not emphasize linguistic polish.
good: We should be careful in not ending up penalizing the people for whom English isn’t the first language or who don’t have English writing skills in their role profile.
why: Use first-person plural (we) and everyday words instead of impersonal passive-sounding policy prose.

bad: While upward stakeholder alignment remains important, a product leader's overarching priority must always anchor on the caliber of the studio's output.
good: You have someone to manage above you too. That’s fine, but remember that your #1 loyalty is the quality of the project in your studio. Nothing has higher priority.
why: Address the reader directly and end on a short, decisive sentence instead of corporate hedging.

bad: Prematurely delegating critical responsibilities to unprepared individuals fosters significant organizational friction across both individual contributors and teams.
good: We are the result of someones trust. Trusting people who are not ready, creates an enormous tension in individuals and in groups.
why: Open with the human truth about trust, then state the consequence for individuals and groups in plain words.

bad: Effective leadership is not about waiting for complete certainty; instead, it requires decisive execution amidst ambiguity.
good: Even when you are not ready or do not know what to do next. Don’t wait for information to “be ready”.
why: Avoid the templated 'is not about X; instead it requires Y' frame; speak directly to the moment of uncertainty.

bad: Challenging one's own assumptions is a vital catalyst for growth, which should be supplemented by cross-functional dialogue with senior peers.
good: It also means that you are questioning yourself and challenging your own thinking. That’s great. Talk to other Leads and colleagues. Producers, Managing Directors.
why: Vary sentence length aggressively (12 words, 2 words, 6 words, 3 words) instead of joining everything with 'which should be supplemented by'.

bad: Unnecessary architectural and procedural complexity invariably impedes operational velocity and detracts from key business outcomes.
good: At the expense of just getting stuff done. Avoidable complexity only hinders work and detracts from results.
why: Say 'getting stuff done' and 'work' instead of 'operational velocity' and 'key business outcomes'.

bad: When evaluating team members, leaders should reflect on whether the individual possessed the requisite context and resources to achieve a superior outcome.
good: Given the context, would the person have been able to do better? Is the person willing to learn from past mistakes? Did they have the proper means to act differently?
why: Use concrete direct questions instead of a flat indirect summary of an evaluation rubric.

bad: As organizational headcount scales beyond Dunbar's number, individual accountability naturally erodes and informal social cohesion begins to fray.
good: People do not at all feel responsible for anything that happens in the larger context, and the social control evaporates. Groups that are larger than 120 usually begin having problems with loyalty e.g.
why: Put people in the subject and name the concrete threshold (120) and problem (loyalty) without academic name-dropping.

bad: Electoral victory does not bestow a mandate to marginalize dissenting constituents; authentic governance demands inclusive stewardship.
good: The role of government and elected leadership is to be inclusive. Winning the elections does not give leadership a carte blanche to disregard the choices and needs of the rest of the population.
why: Lead with what the role of leadership is, and replace 'bestow a mandate / inclusive stewardship' with direct language.

bad: Calculated risk-taking must be harmoniously balanced with a winning mindset, underpinned by rigorous preparation and risk assessment.
good: Risk-taking is finely balanced with another rule, and that is “Play to win”. You don’t have to win all the time, but often. Preparation and risk-assessment is the job of a great leader.
why: Break up abstract participles ('harmoniously balanced, underpinned by') into three clear sentences with a human concession ('not all the time, but often').

bad: The atmosphere in the room felt intensely uncomfortable and tense, as the rhythmic sound echoed loudly through the quiet space.
good: The air in the room is chilling. In the empty cold silence, the drumming is deafening.
why: In scenes, cut emotional labels ('uncomfortable and tense') and weak adverbs ('echoed loudly'); let physical nouns and sensory contrast carry the mood.

bad: One archetype represents an emotionally detached chief executive who operates with machine-like precision and optimizes for multi-century horizons.
good: One is the cold, detached CEO, almost a machine himself, the beyond-transhumanist who thinks over centuries.
why: Use apposition and concrete nouns ('almost a machine himself') rather than sociological labels ('archetype represents... operates with').

bad: Growing up, I was fortunate to have deeply supportive parents who consistently prioritized my educational and personal development.
good: I am deeply grateful to my parents. They were the kind of people who would invest everything in their child.
why: Replace resume-style abstractions ('educational and personal development') with a direct statement of gratitude and who they were.

bad: Servant leadership begins with proactively inquiring how one can alleviate bottlenecks and facilitate daily workflows for the team.
good: Am I helping at the moment? Did you get what you needed? Are there any roadblocks I can remove for you?
why: Replace abstract descriptions of servant leadership with the exact questions you ask a colleague.

bad: On a Tuesday morning, a product manager pastes a half-page note into an AI coding tool and puts a working billing screen on the projector before lunch.
good: Tuesday morning. The product manager pastes a half-page feature note into an AI coding tool and projects a seat-upgrade billing screen twenty minutes later.
why: Drop filler opening prepositions (On a Tuesday morning, a...) and vague artifact labels (working billing screen); open directly in the scene with what the screen does and the exact timing.

bad: Across the table, two engineers ask when the database schema changed, while four recorded user interviews sit unopened in a shared drive. When software takes twenty minutes to mock up, teams mistake a working screen for a settled product decision.
good: Across the table, two engineers lean forward, exchange a tight glance, and ask the product manager when the pricing table and database schema changed. Nobody looks at the four recorded customer interviews sitting unopened in the shared drive. Everyone in the room treats the clickable flow as half-built production code, even though it took twenty minutes to generate and nobody checked whether buyers want self-serve upgrades.
why: Do not compress an opening scene into two rushed AI summary sentences or cite a timing in the analysis that never appeared in the scene; name who asks whom, render posture and glances in the room, and connect the scene directly to the argument.

bad: Three shifts explain what actually changes in the role: discovery work replaces sprint coordination, error analysis on real traces replaces upfront specs, and fast prototypes create opportunity costs and code risks that teams ignore at their peril.
good:
Three shifts explain what changes in the role:
- **Discovery replaces delivery coordination:** AI agents absorb ticket grooming, leaving teams to decide what is worth building.
- **Error analysis replaces upfront specs:** reading real user traces comes before writing automated rubrics.
- **Fast demos still carry hidden costs:** building prototypes steals hours from customer interviews and can ship unvetted code.
why: A list stays a list (Rule 6): render a three-item roadmap as bullet points with bold leads instead of jamming three parallel clauses into one sentence.

bad: Easy prototyping also tempts product managers into building software instead of doing product work, and two practitioner critiques spell out the bill.
good: Easy prototyping also tempts product managers into spending their week coding demos instead of interviewing customers, checking failure traces, and aligning stakeholders on business viability.
why: Never slip in an undefined shorthand concept (product work) that was not in the concept inventory; name the concrete activities directly.

bad: Wednesday, 9:15 a.m. A product manager plugs her laptop into the conference-room screen and opens an interactive billing-dispute assistant she generated in twenty minutes before the meeting.
good: Wednesday, 9:15 a.m. The product manager plugs her laptop into the conference-room screen and opens an interactive billing-dispute assistant she generated in twenty minutes before the meeting.
why: In an opening scene, use the definite article ('The product manager') rather than 'A product manager' to anchor immediately on the central actor in the room.

bad: Nobody in the room opens the folder of forty support tickets exported the evening before.
good: On the corner of the table sits a closed folder of forty support tickets exported the evening before.
why: Never state what nobody does or what is not done; state what physically sits in the room and what people actually do.

bad: When building a clickable screen costs almost nothing, teams mistake a working interface for a settled decision.
good: When building a clickable screen costs almost nothing, teams mistake a working interface for a fully working product, scalable, secure, and handling all the corner cases.
why: Replace vague AI compression ('settled decision') by naming the concrete gap: scalability, security, and corner cases.

bad: Two essays published on November 24, 2026 reacted to the same corporate week from opposite ends of the org chart. On Stratechery, Ben Thompson wrote The Individual Exception, opening with what he built alone in four days using AI agents: a studio control service, single-use iOS apps, and a KVM app.
good: Two essays on November 24, 2026 drew my attention. Ben Thompson wrote in The Individual Exception that he built alone, in four days with AI agents, a studio control service, several iOS apps, and a KVM client.
why: Cut AI thematic introductory wrappers that pre-explain the contrast; when an enumeration needs a lead-in, keep it short and personal without explanation, and tighten participial padding.

bad: Theory gets sharper when checked against live rollouts from late 2026. Three public cases show what agents displace first: cross-team queues and routine sign-offs, well before wholesale layoffs appear.
good: Three late-2026 rollouts caught my eye. All three rely on company-reported numbers, so read the savings with caution.
why: Drop thematic announcer sentences that summarize the punchline before presenting the evidence; use a short personal lead-in or open straight on the first case.

bad: Cheap execution splits management in two directions: how firm-boundary economics and IT studies explain why AI raises solo autonomy while pulling control to the top.
good: Cheap execution splits management in two directions: AI raises solo autonomy at the bottom and pulls control to the top.
why: State roadmap and bullet claims directly instead of padding them as elliptical how/what/why syllabus teasers.
